package_info.package_versions: All supported Windows versions prior to patch (see CVE-2022-30190)
package_info.why_malicious: A path traversal vulnerability in MSDT allows maliciously crafted .diagcab files to copy attacker-controlled executables into the Windows Startup folder, enabling persistent code execution on victim systems.

execution_context.trigger: User opens a maliciously crafted .diagcab file
execution_context.file_location: Malicious .diagcab file processed by MSDT (typically in Downloads or email attachment location)
required_permissions: Write access to the Windows Startup folder (%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup)
Ability to execute MSDT (default for standard users)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The .diagcab file contains a path traversal payload in its internal file references, such as '../../../../../AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/malware.exe', which causes MSDT to extract and write an attacker-supplied executable to the Startup folder.
malicious_snippets.code_language: n/a (exploit via crafted file, not direct code)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a user opens a malicious .diagcab file, MSDT processes the file and, due to a path traversal flaw in file extraction, writes an attacker-supplied executable to the Windows Startup folder, resulting in the executable being launched automatically on the next system reboot.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of path traversal in a diagnostic file to write executables to the Startup folder is highly abnormal and enables persistent code execution without user consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate .diagcab files are intended for diagnostics and troubleshooting, not for writing arbitrary files—especially executables—to sensitive system locations like the Startup folder.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate installers may place shortcuts (not executables) in the Startup folder, but never via diagnostic files or through path traversal exploits.
key_indicators: Presence of path traversal sequences (e.g., '../') in .diagcab file entries
MSDT extracting files to the Startup folder
Unexpected executable files appearing in Startup after opening a .diagcab file
No user prompt or installer process associated with the new Startup entry

attack_chain.action: Victim receives and opens a malicious .diagcab file, typically delivered via phishing email or download.
attack_chain.leads_to: MSDT processes the .diagcab file and, due to a path traversal vulnerability, writes an attacker-controlled executable to the Windows Startup folder.

attack_chain.action: On the next system reboot, the malicious executable in the Startup folder is automatically executed.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent code execution on the victim's system, potentially enabling further compromise or persistence.

behavioral_signatures: MSDT or sdiagnhost.exe processing a .diagcab file results in file creation or modification within the Startup folder
Creation of new executable files in the Startup folder immediately after a .diagcab file is opened
Unusual file extraction activity by MSDT involving path traversal patterns
file_indicators: Presence of unknown or suspicious executables in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup after a .diagcab file is opened
.diagcab files containing file entries with '../' or other path traversal sequences
Timestamps on Startup folder executables closely following .diagcab file access
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for MSDT (sdiagnhost.exe) or related processes writing files to the Startup folder, especially following the opening of .diagcab files. Flag .diagcab files that contain path traversal sequences in their internal file paths or reference the Startup folder. Alert on the creation of new executables in the Startup folder that are not associated with legitimate software installations or updates. Correlate file creation events with recent .diagcab file activity to identify potential exploitation.
